a.title: A Day for Animals
text: October 4 is World Animal Day. It is a day to think about animals and how we treat them.
Animals share our world. Some live in our homes, like cats and dogs. Others live in forests, oceans, and the sky.
On this day, people learn how to care for animals. They talk about pets, farm animals, and wild animals in danger.
Many animals need our help. Some lose their homes when forests are cut down. Some need a kind family to adopt them.
You can help too. Be gentle with pets. Give them food, water, and love. Never leave an animal alone in the cold.
When we are kind to animals, the whole world becomes a better home for everyone.

b.title: Sharing the Planet
text: Every year on 4 October, people mark World Animal Day, a global event that asks a simple question: how well do we treat the creatures we share the planet with?
The date honours Saint Francis of Assisi, a man remembered for his love of animals. Today it is used to raise awareness of animal welfare all over the world.

The concerns are wide. Pets are sometimes abandoned when families no longer want them. Farm animals are often kept in poor conditions. And in the wild, many species are losing their homes as forests are cleared and the climate warms.

There is also good news. Animal shelters find new homes for millions of pets each year, and laws in many countries now protect animals from cruelty. Some once-endangered species have slowly recovered.
Small choices matter. Adopting a pet instead of buying one, supporting local shelters, and simply treating animals with respect all make a difference.
The message of the day is gentle but important: animals cannot speak for themselves, so it is up to people to speak, and act, for them.

c.title: The Creatures We Live Among
text: Each 4 October, World Animal Day invites a reckoning of sorts: an annual pause to ask what humans owe the millions of other species with which they share a crowded planet.

The day traces its spirit to Saint Francis of Assisi, the medieval friar who spoke of animals as brothers and sisters. Yet its modern purpose is less devotional than practical — to focus attention on animal welfare, from the family pet to the vanishing tiger.

The moral landscape is complicated. Few people wish animals harm, and yet human choices — what we eat, what we buy, how we build — shape the fate of countless creatures we will never see. Habitat loss, driven by farming and a warming climate, remains the greatest threat to wild species.

Progress, where it exists, tends to be quiet. Stronger animal-protection laws, the steady work of shelters and sanctuaries, and shifting attitudes toward adoption have all improved millions of individual lives, even as the larger picture stays fragile.

Perhaps that is the day's real lesson: that kindness to animals is not sentimentality but a measure of a society's character, and that a species clever enough to reshape the Earth bears some responsibility for the others living on it.

a.title: Turning Brain Cells On with Light
text: On October 5, 2026, three scientists won the Nobel Prize in Medicine. Their names are Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann, and Georg Nagel.
They found a way to control brain cells with light. This idea is called optogenetics.
The brain has billions of tiny cells. These cells send signals that make us move, think, and feel.
The scientists took a special protein from algae — tiny green plants that live in water. This protein reacts to light.
They put the protein inside brain cells. Now, when light shines on a cell, the cell turns on. When the light stops, the cell turns off.
This tool helps scientists understand the brain. One day, it may even help blind people see again.

b.title: Optogenetics: Switching Neurons On and Off
text: On 5 October 2026, the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was awarded to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann, and Georg Nagel for a powerful technique known as optogenetics.

The brain is made of billions of nerve cells, or neurons, that communicate using tiny electrical signals. For a long time, scientists could watch these signals, but they could not switch a single neuron on or off whenever they wanted.
The breakthrough began with green algae. Hegemann and Nagel discovered that these simple organisms carry light-sensitive proteins called channelrhodopsins, which open when light hits them.
Deisseroth then had a bold idea: place these proteins inside neurons. Shine a blue light, and the neuron fires; take the light away, and it falls silent — all within milliseconds.
This gave researchers a precise 'switch' for the brain. By turning chosen neurons on and off, they can study how brain circuits control movement, memory, and mood.
Optogenetics is also moving toward medicine. In one remarkable case reported in Nature Medicine, light-sensitive proteins helped restore partial vision to a man who had been blind for decades.

c.title: A Light Switch for the Mind
text: When the Nobel Assembly announced the 2026 Prize in Physiology or Medicine on 5 October, it honoured a discovery that has quietly transformed neuroscience: optogenetics, the art of controlling individual neurons with nothing more than a beam of light.

The award was shared equally by Karl Deisseroth of Stanford University, and Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel of Germany. Their work answered a question that had frustrated researchers for generations — how to study the living brain not by observing it, but by commanding it.

The key came from an unlikely source: pond-dwelling green algae. Hegemann and Nagel showed that these microbes steer toward light using proteins called channelrhodopsins, molecular gates that spring open the instant light strikes them.

Deisseroth's insight was to borrow these gates and install them in mammalian neurons. A pulse of blue light could now make a chosen neuron fire, while darkness silenced it — with a speed and precision that earlier methods could never match.

The consequences were profound. Because behaviour, emotion and memory all arise from the firing of particular circuits, scientists could finally test cause and effect directly, switching circuits on and off to see exactly what each one does.

The technique is now reaching the clinic. In a landmark trial published in Nature Medicine, optogenetic therapy restored a measure of sight to a patient blinded by an inherited eye disease — a hint of future treatments for blindness, paralysis and disorders of the brain.

a.title: Thank You, Teachers
text: October 5 is World Teachers' Day. It is a day to say thank you to teachers everywhere.
Teachers help us learn to read, write, count, and think. They also teach us how to be kind and work with others.
A good teacher does more than give lessons. They listen, they care, and they help students believe in themselves.
Being a teacher is not easy. They work long hours, plan lessons, and worry about every student.
In many countries, there are not enough teachers. The world needs millions more so that every child can go to school.
On this day, we say two small but powerful words to our teachers: thank you.

b.title: The People Who Shape Us
text: Each year on 5 October, UNESCO leads the world in celebrating World Teachers' Day, a moment to honour the people who quietly shape every other profession.
Teachers do far more than deliver facts. They spark curiosity, build confidence, and are often the first adults outside the family to believe in a child's future.

Yet the job is under strain. Many teachers work long unpaid hours, face crowded classrooms, and earn less than others with similar training. In some places, respect for the profession has slowly faded.
The world also faces a shortage. The United Nations estimates that tens of millions of new teachers are needed so that every child can receive a decent education, especially in poorer regions.
Technology is changing the classroom too. Useful tools, and even AI, can support teaching, but few believe they can replace the patience, warmth, and judgement of a real teacher.
The day's message is simple: a society that wants a better future must value, support, and fairly pay the people it trusts to build it.

c.title: In Praise of the Teacher
text: On 5 October the world observes World Teachers' Day, an occasion easy to sentimentalise and just as easy to overlook. Behind the greeting cards lies a serious claim: that no profession does more to determine a nation's future, and few are asked to do so much with so little.

The work resists measurement. A teacher's influence — a question that sparks a career, a word of belief on a hard day — often surfaces years later, in lives the teacher never sees. What can be measured tells a harder story: rising workloads, stagnant pay, and, in many places, a slow erosion of public respect.

The result is a global shortage. UNESCO warns that the world needs tens of millions more teachers to meet its education goals, a gap widest precisely where schooling is most needed. Recruiting them is one thing; keeping them, when so many leave within a few years, is another.

Into this arrives technology, promising to lighten the load. Well-designed tools can indeed help, but the enthusiasm for automation can obscure a stubborn truth: learning is relational. A screen can deliver information; it cannot notice the quiet child at the back of the room.
That, in the end, is what the day defends — not a job title, but a human relationship on which almost everything else depends.

a.title: A Giant Telescope Made of Ice
text: On October 6, 2026, a scientist named Francis Halzen won the Nobel Prize in Physics.
He helped build IceCube, a huge detector deep in the ice of Antarctica, near the South Pole.
IceCube hunts for tiny particles called neutrinos. They are so small that they fly right through you — and through the whole Earth!
Trillions of neutrinos pass through your body every second, but you never feel them.
Once in a while, a neutrino hits the ice and makes a tiny blue flash of light. Thousands of sensors in the ice can see it.
Some neutrinos come from faraway, powerful events in space. By catching them, scientists can study the universe in a brand-new way.

b.title: IceCube: Hunting Ghost Particles at the South Pole
text: On 6 October 2026, the Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to Francis Halzen for his leading role in the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos from space.

Neutrinos are among the strangest particles in nature. They have almost no mass, carry no electric charge, and hardly ever bump into anything. Trillions stream through your body every second without leaving a trace.
That makes them incredibly hard to catch. To do it, scientists turned a cubic kilometre of clear Antarctic ice into a detector, burying over 5,000 light sensors deep beneath the South Pole.
Now and then, a neutrino crashes into the ice and creates a faint blue glow. The sensors record this light and reveal where the particle came from.
In 2013, IceCube found the first neutrinos born far beyond our solar system, in some of the most violent events in the universe.
Because neutrinos travel in straight lines and pass through almost everything, they carry clues that ordinary light cannot. Halzen's work opened a new field: neutrino astronomy.

c.title: Reading the Universe with Neutrinos
text: When the Royal Swedish Academy named Francis Halzen the 2026 Nobel laureate in Physics on 6 October, it recognised a discovery that gave astronomers an entirely new sense: the ability to 'see' the cosmos through neutrinos.
Neutrinos are nature's great escape artists. Nearly massless and electrically neutral, they interact so weakly that most slip through the entire Earth as though it were empty space.

Capturing them demanded an instrument of extraordinary scale. Under Halzen's leadership, the IceCube Observatory transformed a cubic kilometre of pristine Antarctic ice into a detector, threaded with thousands of sensors more than a kilometre below the surface.

On the rare occasion that a neutrino strikes an atom in the ice, it releases a ghostly blue flash. From the pattern of light, scientists can reconstruct the particle's energy and trace its path back across the sky.
In 2013, IceCube detected the first high-energy neutrinos of cosmic origin, later linking some to distant galaxies with supermassive black holes at their hearts.

Unlike light, neutrinos stream unblocked from the universe's most hidden and violent corners. Halzen's achievement founded neutrino astronomy, opening a fresh window onto events no ordinary telescope could ever observe.

a.title: Molecules That Come in Two Hands
text: On October 7, 2026, two scientists won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Their names are Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai.
Hold up your two hands. They look the same, but they are mirror images — a left and a right. You cannot put a left glove on your right hand.

This really matters for medicine. Often only one hand helps your body. The other hand may do nothing — or even cause harm.

b.title: Left-Handed and Right-Handed Molecules
text: On 7 October 2026, the Nobel Prize in Chemistry went to Henri Kagan of France and Kenso Soai of Japan for work on 'asymmetric synthesis' — building molecules with a chosen handedness.
Just as your left and right hands are mirror images that cannot overlap, many molecules exist in two mirror-image forms, which chemists call 'left' and 'right'.
Inside living bodies, the two forms can behave completely differently. One form of a drug may heal, while its mirror twin does nothing — or causes side effects.
For a long time, ordinary reactions made both forms in equal amounts, and separating them afterwards was slow and costly.
Kagan discovered that a small amount of a one-handed 'helper', called a catalyst, could steer a reaction to produce far more of a single form — a surprising amplifying effect.

Soai went further, creating a reaction that makes a product which then helps make more of itself. A tiny imbalance at the start grows into an almost perfectly one-handed result — a powerful tool for cleaner, safer medicines.

c.title: The Chemistry of Handedness
text: When the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry on 7 October, it honoured Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai for taming one of chemistry's most elegant puzzles: handedness.
Countless molecules are 'chiral' — they exist as two mirror images, like a pair of hands, that can never be laid perfectly on top of each other. The two versions are known as enantiomers.

In biology, the distinction is anything but trivial. The receptors in our cells are themselves handed, so one enantiomer of a drug may cure a patient while its mirror image is useless, or even dangerous.
Ordinary reactions, however, tend to produce the two forms in equal measure. The challenge was to tip the balance — to make one hand far more often than the other.

Kagan showed that this could be done with startling efficiency: a catalyst only slightly biased toward one hand could yield a product overwhelmingly of that hand, a counter-intuitive 'non-linear' effect.

Soai then revealed something close to chemical magic — a self-replicating, or autocatalytic, reaction in which the product speeds up its own formation, amplifying a faint initial imbalance into near-perfect purity. Together, their insights underpin the clean, precise synthesis of modern medicines.

Carson is both a poet and a scholar of ancient Greek. For her, writers who lived thousands of years ago — like the poet Sappho — are living voices, not dusty books.

c.title: In Playful Dialogue with the Ancients
text: When the Swedish Academy named Anne Carson the 2026 Nobel laureate in Literature on 8 October, it celebrated a writer who has spent her life in conversation with the distant past.
A Canadian poet, essayist, and professor of classics, Carson treats the ancient Greeks not as relics to be studied, but as companions to argue and play with.
Her signature work, 'Autobiography of Red', reimagines an obscure myth — the red, winged monster Geryon — as a luminous coming-of-age story written as a novel in verse.
Across her career she has dissolved the borders between genres, weaving together poetry, scholarship, and memoir; her elegy 'Nox' arrives as a single folded page in a box, part book, part object.
As a translator, she renders the surviving fragments of Sappho with their losses intact, letting the blank spaces speak as loudly as the words.

The Academy honoured her 'bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature' — proof that the oldest voices can still sound startlingly new.

c.title: Building Peace Through Law
text: When the Norwegian Nobel Committee awarded the 2026 Peace Prize to Navi Pillay on 9 October, it recognised a lifetime spent insisting that justice belongs to everyone, not only the powerful.

Born in 1941 into a working-class family in South Africa, Pillay came of age under apartheid, a system that stripped most of the population of basic rights. Education became her way out — and her weapon.
She became the first non-white woman to open a law practice in her province, often defending opponents of the regime when few others dared.

Her reach grew global. As a judge, and later president, of the international tribunal for Rwanda, she helped establish that rape could be prosecuted as a crime of genocide — a landmark for international justice.
From 2008 to 2014 she served as the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, a fearless voice for the persecuted regardless of politics or borders.
Her career embodies a quiet but radical idea: that lasting peace rests on the rule of law, and that protecting the rights of the weakest protects us all.

a.title: The City the Volcano Buried
text: Pompeii was a busy Roman city in Italy, almost two thousand years ago. People lived, worked, and shopped there every day.
Near the city stood a mountain called Mount Vesuvius. The people did not know it was a dangerous volcano.
In the year 79, the volcano erupted. It threw ash and rock high into the sky for two days.
The whole city was buried under deep ash. Sadly, many people could not escape in time.
For hundreds of years, Pompeii lay hidden and forgotten. Then, much later, people dug it up again.
Today we can walk through its streets and houses. Pompeii shows us exactly how Romans lived long ago.

b.title: A Day That Stopped Forever
text: Nearly two thousand years ago, Pompeii was a lively Roman town near the bay of Naples, in Italy — home to shops, baths, theatres, and around twelve thousand people.
Looming above it was Mount Vesuvius. Few people realised that the green mountain was in fact a sleeping volcano.
In AD 79, Vesuvius exploded with terrible force. For two days it rained ash and burning rock, until the town — and many who had stayed behind — lay buried under metres of volcanic debris.
Terrible as it was, the ash also preserved the city. Buildings, wall paintings, loaves of bread, and even the shapes of people were sealed and protected underground for centuries.
Rediscovered and slowly excavated from the 1700s onward, Pompeii became a window into the ancient world. Archaeologists could read shop signs, study homes, and learn what Romans ate and wore.
Vesuvius is still active today, and scientists watch it closely. Pompeii remains a haunting reminder of nature's power — and a priceless record of a single ancient day.

c.title: The Gift of Catastrophe
text: Among the ironies of history, few are sharper than Pompeii: a catastrophe that destroyed a city and, in the same stroke, saved it. When Mount Vesuvius erupted in AD 79, it ended thousands of lives; it also sealed an entire Roman town beneath a blanket of ash, pausing it, mid-gesture, for nearly two millennia.

What makes Pompeii extraordinary is not grandeur but ordinariness. Rome left behind temples and monuments by design; Pompeii left behind the unguarded everyday — graffiti scratched on walls, election posters, a dog chained in a doorway, a meal abandoned on a table. The eruption froze not emperors but ordinary people, caught in an ordinary morning.

The ash proved a cruel kind of preservative. By packing tightly around bodies that later decayed, it left hollow moulds; when archaeologists poured plaster into these voids, the victims' final postures emerged — figures crouching, shielding children, holding one another.
Such discoveries raise uneasy questions about how we study the dead. Pompeii is at once a scientific treasure and a mass grave, and the line between learning and intrusion is not always clear.
Still, the town endures as our most vivid link to antiquity — proof that the smallest details of a vanished life can outlast the empires that once seemed so much more permanent.

a.title: Welcome to Kyoto
text: Kyoto is a beautiful old city in Japan. For more than a thousand years, it was the country's capital.
Kyoto is famous for its temples and shrines. Some are made of wood and are very, very old.
One famous place is Fushimi Inari, where thousands of bright orange gates stand in a long line up a hill.
In spring, pink cherry blossoms cover the city. In autumn, the leaves turn red and gold. Many people visit just to see them.
In the old streets of Gion, you might see a geisha in a beautiful kimono walking quietly by.
Kyoto mixes the old and the new. It is a wonderful place to learn about Japanese history and culture.

b.title: A City of a Thousand Years
text: For over a thousand years, until 1868, Kyoto was the capital of Japan. Though Tokyo holds that title now, Kyoto remains the nation's cultural heart.

The city is home to around two thousand temples and shrines. At Kiyomizu-dera, a wooden hall stands on tall pillars over a hillside; at Fushimi Inari, thousands of vermilion gates form glowing tunnels up the mountain.
Kyoto changes beautifully with the seasons. Spring brings clouds of cherry blossom; autumn sets the maples of Arashiyama ablaze in red and orange. These two seasons draw by far the largest crowds.
The old district of Gion is famous for its wooden tea houses and its geisha, women trained for years in traditional dance, music, and the art of conversation.
Visitors can still enjoy a simple cup of matcha tea, a quiet temple garden, or a meal of local tofu and vegetables.
Above all, Kyoto asks to be taken slowly. It rewards those who wander its back streets and pause to notice small, carefully made beauty.

c.title: The Art of Going Slowly
text: To arrive in Kyoto expecting a museum is to misread it. Japan's capital for more than a millennium, the city wears its history not as a relic under glass but as a living habit — in the rhythm of its seasons, the manners of its streets, and a quiet insistence on doing things with care.

Its set-piece treasures are rightly famous: the vermilion corridors of Fushimi Inari, the hillside stage of Kiyomizu-dera, the towering bamboo groves of Arashiyama. Yet the first-time visitor, hurrying between them with a guidebook, often misses what makes Kyoto itself — the unhurried attention it pays to small things.

That attention shows everywhere: in a bowl of tea whisked just so, in a raked gravel garden meant to be contemplated rather than entered, in the training of a geisha measured not in weeks but in years.
Modern Kyoto, of course, also has traffic, convenience stores, and crowds that strain its most delicate corners, raising hard questions about how a living city can carry so priceless a past.
Perhaps that is Kyoto's deepest lesson for the traveller — and a useful one anywhere: that beauty is often found not by seeing more, but by slowing down enough to notice what was already there.

a.title: Keeping Prices and Jobs Steady

b.title: The Science of a Stable Economy
text: On 12 October 2026, Robert Hall and Michael Woodford won the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences for their work on the 'microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation'.
That long phrase hides a simple question: how do the everyday choices of millions of people and businesses add up to the ups and downs of a whole country's economy?
When prices rise too quickly, savings lose value; when demand falls, factories close and workers lose their jobs. Governments want to avoid both.
Hall and Woodford built careful models showing how people's spending, saving, and especially their expectations about the future shape the bigger picture.
Their work gave central banks a firmer basis for using tools like interest rates to steer the economy between overheating and slowing down.
Because of ideas like theirs, the banks that guard our money can act with more confidence when they try to keep prices stable and jobs plentiful.

c.title: From Small Choices to the Whole Economy
text: On 12 October 2026, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awarded the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences to Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford 'for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation'.

Macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole — inflation, unemployment, growth — while microeconomics studies the decisions of single households and firms. The laureates helped bind the two together.

Their central insight is that the great swings of a national economy grow out of countless individual choices: how much to spend or save, what prices to set, and above all, what people expect to happen next.
Woodford showed how a central bank's words and credibility shape those expectations, so that guiding what people believe about future inflation can be as powerful as any single change in rates.
Hall illuminated how labour markets and spending respond over the business cycle, clarifying why recessions deepen and how recoveries take hold.

Together, their rigorous models turned central banking from something of an art into something far closer to a science, underpinning how institutions today fight both runaway prices and painful slumps.

b.title: Where the Earth Is Still Being Made
text: Few countries feel as otherworldly as Iceland, a volcanic island near the Arctic Circle where fire and ice share the same landscape.
The island sits where two of Earth's great plates pull apart, so volcanoes and earthquakes are common. At the same time, vast glaciers cover much of the interior.
This restless geology is also a gift. Heat from underground warms homes and fills open-air pools such as the famous Blue Lagoon, even in freezing weather.
Nature is never far away. The 'Golden Circle' route takes visitors past a thundering waterfall, erupting hot springs, and a rift valley where two continents slowly split.
In the long winter nights, the sky sometimes glows with the aurora — curtains of green and violet light; in summer, by contrast, the sun barely sets at all.
With a tiny population and enormous open spaces, Iceland offers travellers something rare: the chance to feel the raw power of the planet up close.

c.title: Living on the Seam of the World
text: To travel in Iceland is to be reminded, constantly, that the ground beneath us is alive. The island straddles the boundary between two tectonic plates, and so it is forever being torn apart and built anew — a country, in effect, under construction.

This gives the landscape its strange grandeur: lava fields still black and bare, geysers that fire boiling water skyward, glaciers grinding whole valleys into shape. It also gives Icelanders a practical bargain with the earth, drawing clean heat and power from the volcanic rock below.

That intimacy with nature shapes the culture. A nation of fewer than four hundred thousand people has produced a fierce literary tradition, a deep love of storytelling, and — famously — a lingering half-seriousness about elves said to live in the rocks.

Tourism, now vital to the economy, brings its own tensions: fragile moss and quiet places can be worn away by too many feet, and Icelanders openly debate how to welcome the world without losing what makes the island special.
Still, few places teach the traveller so plainly that the planet is not a fixed stage but a living, moving thing — and that we are, all of us, only its temporary guests.

a.title: A Robot Driver on Mars
text: On Mars, a NASA robot car called Perseverance explores a dry, rocky world far from Earth.
Mars is about 140 million miles away. A message from Earth takes many minutes to arrive.
Because of this delay, drivers on Earth cannot steer the rover in real time.
In December 2025, something new happened. For the first time, artificial intelligence — AI — planned the rover's path by itself.
The AI looked at pictures of the ground taken from space. It found rocks, sand, and safe places to drive, then drew a route.
The rover followed the plan and drove hundreds of metres. NASA shared the exciting results in January 2026.

b.title: AI Takes the Wheel on Mars
text: In December 2025, NASA's Perseverance rover did something no spacecraft had done before: it drove along a route planned entirely by artificial intelligence. NASA announced the results in January 2026.
Driving on Mars is tricky. The planet is about 225 million kilometres away, so radio signals take many minutes each way. Steering the rover live from Earth is impossible.
For 28 years, human engineers have carefully sketched each route by hand, marking points where the rover stops to receive new instructions.

This time, a kind of generative AI studied high-resolution photos taken from orbit, together with maps of the slopes. It recognised bedrock, boulders, and ripples of sand, then designed a smooth path.
Before sending the plan to Mars, engineers tested it on a 'digital twin' — a virtual copy of the rover — checking hundreds of thousands of details.
The rover then rolled safely across Jezero Crater. One day, AI could let explorers on other worlds make quick decisions on their own.

c.title: When a Rover Plans Its Own Path
text: In January 2026, NASA revealed a quiet milestone in space exploration: the previous December, its Perseverance rover had completed the first drives on another world mapped out not by people, but by artificial intelligence.

The challenge is distance. With Mars roughly 225 million kilometres from Earth, radio commands arrive many minutes late, making real-time control impossible. For nearly three decades, engineers have plotted every route by hand, waypoint by waypoint.
The new approach used a form of generative AI known as vision-language models. The system examined sharp images from a Mars orbiter and detailed maps of the terrain's slopes.
From that data it identified bedrock, boulder fields, and ripples of sand, then stitched together a continuous, safe path — spacing its waypoints far more widely than human planners usually dare.
Nothing was sent blindly. The commands were first rehearsed on a 'digital twin', a virtual replica of the rover, where engineers checked over half a million measurements.
The drives, covering several hundred metres across Jezero Crater, hint at a future in which distant robots — and perhaps astronauts — navigate strange landscapes with far less help from home.

a.title: The Night the Wall Came Down
text: For 28 years, a long concrete wall cut the city of Berlin in two. On one side was East Germany; on the other, West Germany.
The wall was built in 1961. Families and friends were suddenly split apart. Many could not visit each other for years.
The two sides lived very differently. The West was free and rich; the East was ruled by a strict government with much less freedom.
People in the East wanted change. In 1989, huge but peaceful crowds marched in the streets.
On November 9, 1989, the government finally opened the gates. Crowds climbed the wall, hugged, and cried with joy.
People broke the wall apart with hammers. That night changed Germany — and the world — forever.

b.title: A Wall, and the People Who Ended It
text: For nearly three decades, the Berlin Wall was the world's most famous symbol of division. Built in 1961, it sealed off communist East Germany from the free, democratic West, cutting straight through the heart of Berlin.
The wall was more than concrete. Guards, fences, and watchtowers stopped East Germans from fleeing west, and some who tried were killed. Families were separated for a generation.
By 1989, pressure was building across Eastern Europe. Reforms in the Soviet Union and brave, peaceful protests in East German cities made the old rulers look weak.
Then, on the evening of November 9, 1989, a confused government announcement suggested the border was open. Thousands rushed to the crossings, and the overwhelmed guards simply raised the barriers.
What followed was pure celebration. Strangers embraced, people danced on top of the wall, and crowds began to chip it away with hammers and chisels.
Less than a year later, East and West Germany were reunited. The fall of the wall came to stand for the peaceful end of the Cold War in Europe.

c.title: The Night History Turned
text: Some walls are built to keep enemies out; the Berlin Wall was built to keep a population in. For twenty-eight years it stood as the Cold War made concrete — a 155-kilometre scar dividing not only a city but two visions of how human beings should live.

Its fall, on the night of 9 November 1989, was almost an accident. A muddled press conference, a misread note, a spokesman's uncertain words — and suddenly East Germans were walking, unhindered, toward checkpoints that had meant death to cross. The guards, awaiting orders that never came, stepped aside.

What makes the night remarkable is less the politics than the restraint. A heavily armed border, decades of resentment, vast crowds — and yet almost no violence. The revolution was carried out with hammers against stone, not against people.
The consequences were immense: Germany reunified within a year, the Soviet bloc dissolved, and the long standoff that had shadowed the twentieth century quietly ended.

Yet the wall also leaves a warning. It was raised in a single night and took a generation to fall — a reminder of how quickly freedom can be enclosed, and how much courage, and patience, it can take to open it again.

a.title: Chang'e Flies to the Moon
text: Long ago in China, there were ten suns in the sky. They burned the land, and the people suffered.

b.title: The Lady in the Moon
text: One of China's best-loved myths explains the shape many people see in the full moon. It begins with a sky scorched by ten suns.
A heroic archer, Houyi, saved the world by shooting down nine of them. For this, the gods rewarded him with an elixir of immortality — enough for one person to live forever.
Houyi loved his wife, Chang'e, and did not want to leave her behind, so he hid the elixir at home. But one day, while he was away, a greedy student tried to steal it.
To stop the thief, Chang'e swallowed the elixir herself. She became weightless and drifted up into the sky, finally coming to rest on the cold, silver moon.
There she has lived ever since, the stories say, with only a jade rabbit for company — forever near the world she loved, yet unable to return to it.
Each Mid-Autumn Festival, families gaze at the round moon and think of Chang'e: a tale of love, sacrifice, and the ache of separation.

c.title: What We See in the Moon
text: Every culture that has gazed at the moon has told stories to explain its marks. In China, those marks are Chang'e — a goddess whose legend turns a bright object in the sky into an image of longing.

The tale is deceptively simple. Her husband, the archer Houyi, wins an elixir of immortality; to keep it from a thief, Chang'e drinks it herself and floats, irreversibly, to the moon. What begins as a rescue ends as an exile.

The myth's power lies in its ambivalence. Chang'e gains eternal life but loses everything that made life worth living — her home, her husband, the warm and ordinary world below. Immortality, the story quietly suggests, can be its own kind of prison.

That is perhaps why the legend binds itself so naturally to the Mid-Autumn Festival, a celebration of reunion. Families gathered beneath the full moon are reminded, by the lonely figure within it, of exactly what they have — and how precious togetherness is.
A myth, in the end, is a mirror held up to a people's values. In Chang'e, China sees not only a goddess, but a meditation on sacrifice, distance, and the bittersweet cost of living forever.

b.title: Enough for All?
text: Every year on 16 October, the United Nations marks World Food Day, led by its Food and Agriculture Organization, or FAO. The date asks an uncomfortable question: why, on a planet that grows plenty, do so many still go hungry?
The numbers are stark. Hundreds of millions of people do not get enough to eat, and hunger has risen in recent years because of conflict, drought, and high prices.
Waste makes the problem worse. Studies suggest that roughly a third of all food produced is lost or thrown away — spoiled on farms, damaged in transport, or scraped off plates in wealthy homes.

The causes are tangled, but solutions exist. Farmers can grow crops that survive a changing climate, shops and families can waste less, and fairer systems can help food reach the people who need it most.
Food is also about health and culture. A good meal is not only fuel; it brings families together and carries the taste of home.
The message of World Food Day is both practical and hopeful: there is enough for everyone, if only we grow, share, and value it wisely.

c.title: The Paradox of the Full Plate
text: Each 16 October the United Nations observes World Food Day, an occasion built around a paradox: humanity grows more than enough food to feed itself, and yet hundreds of millions remain hungry.

The contradiction deepens on closer look. Even as some go without, roughly a third of all food produced is never eaten — lost to poor storage in poorer countries, and to sheer waste in richer ones. The world, in effect, starves and squanders at the same time.

Hunger is rarely a simple shortage of food; more often it is a failure of access. War drives families from their fields, drought ruins harvests, and inflation puts the market stall beyond reach. Where food is treated purely as a commodity, those with the least money eat last.

None of this is beyond human repair. Hardier crops, better storage, shorter supply chains, and policies that treat food as a right rather than a privilege could, together, narrow the gap. So could a cultural shift away from waste in kitchens and supermarkets alike.
World Food Day, at its best, refuses an easy despair. It insists that hunger in an age of plenty is not a natural disaster but a human choice — and therefore one that humans can unmake.

b.title: The Eternal City
text: Rome, the capital of Italy, has been called the 'Eternal City' for two thousand years — and it wears its age proudly.
At its height, ancient Rome ruled much of Europe, North Africa, and the Middle East. The remains of that empire still fill the modern streets.
The Colosseum, a vast arena that once held fifty thousand spectators, remains the city's most famous monument. Nearby lie the ruins of the Forum, the beating heart of the ancient city.
Rome is also layered with art and faith. Within it sits the Vatican, home of the Pope, where visitors line up to see Michelangelo's painted ceiling in the Sistine Chapel.
Yet Rome is no museum. Scooters weave through narrow lanes, markets spill across old squares, and families argue happily over plates of pasta.
To walk through Rome is to walk through time itself — from a Roman temple, to a Renaissance church, to a modern café, often within a single street.

c.title: A City Built on Itself
text: No city carries its past quite like Rome. Three thousand years of history are not neatly preserved here but piled up, layer upon layer, so that an ancient temple may support a medieval church that now shades a modern bus stop.

The scale of the old city still astonishes. The Colosseum, where crowds once roared at gladiators, and the Pantheon, whose vast dome has stood unbroken for nearly nineteen centuries, remind visitors that the Romans built not merely for their own age but, it seems, for all of them.
Layered atop the empire is another Rome — the spiritual capital of the Catholic world, its skyline crowned by the dome of St Peter's, its galleries holding some of the greatest art ever made.
To live among such grandeur is a daily negotiation. Romans complain, fairly, of crowds, traffic, and the burden of maintaining a city that belongs, in a sense, to the whole world.
And yet the city endures, as it always has — not by freezing its past, but by living inside it, turning ruins into backdrops and history into the ordinary scenery of everyday life.

a.title: The Boy Who Flew Too High
text: Long ago, in an old Greek story, a clever man named Daedalus and his son Icarus were trapped on an island.
To escape, Daedalus made two big pairs of wings. He joined feathers together with soft wax.
Before they flew, Daedalus warned his son. “Do not fly too low, or the sea will wet your wings. Do not fly too high, or the sun will melt the wax.”
At first, Icarus was careful. But flying felt wonderful, and soon he forgot his father's words.
He flew higher and higher, close to the sun. The wax melted, his wings fell apart, and Icarus dropped into the sea.
People still tell this story today. It teaches us to be brave — but also to listen, and to know our limits.

b.title: Between the Sea and the Sun
text: One of the most famous of all Greek myths tells of Daedalus, a brilliant inventor, and his son Icarus, imprisoned on the island of Crete by King Minos.
Daedalus devised a daring escape. From feathers and wax he built two great pairs of wings, so that he and his son might simply fly away.
He gave Icarus one firm warning: fly a middle course. Too low, and the sea's spray would weigh the feathers down; too high, and the sun's heat would melt the wax.
For a while the plan worked, and the two rose into the open sky. But Icarus, thrilled by the sheer power of flight, ignored his father and soared ever upward toward the sun.
The wax softened, the feathers loosened, and the boy plunged into the sea that still bears his name. Daedalus flew on alone, grief-stricken.
For thousands of years the tale has been read as a warning against pride and recklessness — yet some also see in Icarus the beauty of daring to reach for something far greater than yourself.

c.title: The Two Lessons of Icarus
text: Few images from mythology have proved as enduring as the fall of Icarus: a boy, feathered wings melting, dropping from a bright sky into an indifferent sea. For nearly three thousand years the Greek tale has been retold, painted, and argued over — chiefly because it refuses to mean only one thing.

The conventional reading is a caution against hubris. Warned by his father Daedalus to keep a middle course, Icarus flew too close to the sun, and his pride — or his carelessness — destroyed him. In this version the moral is restraint: know your limits, and heed those wiser than you.

Yet a second reading has grown louder in modern times. Icarus, after all, did what humankind had only dreamed of — he flew. If his reach exceeded his grasp, perhaps the reaching itself was glorious, and a life spent hugging the safe middle is its own kind of failure.

Tellingly, the myth gives us both a reckless son and a cautious father, and it is the son we remember. Daedalus survives, yet it is Icarus whose name endures — as if the story cannot quite decide whether to mourn his fall or admire his flight.
That unresolved tension is the myth's genius. It hands each listener a mirror and asks a question as old as ambition itself: how high is too high?

topic: La Tomatina: The Great Tomato Fight
zh: 番茄節：西班牙丟番茄大戰

a.title: The Great Tomato Fight
text: In a small town in Spain called Buñol, there is one very messy festival. It is called La Tomatina.
On the last Wednesday of August, thousands of people meet in the town square. They all want to throw tomatoes!
Big trucks bring in piles of soft, ripe tomatoes — more than one hundred tons of them.

b.title: A Town Painted Red
text: Once a year, the quiet Spanish town of Buñol, near Valencia, turns bright red. On the last Wednesday of August, it hosts La Tomatina, the world's biggest food fight.
Around twenty thousand people pack the narrow streets — far more than the town's own population. Trucks arrive loaded with over a hundred tons of ripe tomatoes.
At a signal, the battle begins. For one glorious, chaotic hour, strangers hurl tomatoes at anyone within reach, until the streets run with red pulp.
There are a few rules. Tomatoes must be squashed before they are thrown, so they cannot injure anyone, and the fight stops the moment a second signal sounds.
No one is quite sure how it began — perhaps a street scuffle among young people in 1945 — but the tradition stuck, and today it draws visitors from all over the world.
Afterwards, the townspeople hose down the streets, and the tomato juice leaves the old stones unusually clean. The mess, it turns out, washes away easily — and the memories last.

c.title: The Serious Business of Play
text: To an outsider, La Tomatina looks like pure chaos: twenty thousand people, a hundred tons of tomatoes, and one hour of cheerful violence in the streets of a small Spanish town. Yet beneath the mess lies something worth taking seriously — the human need to play.

The festival's origins are humble and uncertain, probably a spontaneous squabble among young people in 1945 that was simply repeated the next year, and the next, until accident hardened into tradition.

What endures is not meaning but release. In everyday life we are told to be careful, clean, and controlled; for one hour, La Tomatina suspends all of that, inviting ordinary adults to be gleefully ridiculous with the full permission of their town.
There is even a quiet logic to the tomato. Soft, cheap, and harmless once squashed, it allows a kind of combat with no real victims — aggression turned entirely into joy.

Every culture builds such safety valves, from carnivals to festivals of colour. La Tomatina is simply one of the loudest: proof that a community sometimes needs, together, to make a glorious and meaningless mess — and then wash it clean.

a.title: The Slowest Animal in the Trees
text: October 20 is International Sloth Day. It is a day to learn about one of the slowest animals in the world.
Sloths live in the rainforests of Central and South America. They spend almost all their life high up in the trees.
A sloth moves very slowly. It hangs upside down from branches with its long, curved claws.
Sloths eat leaves. Leaves do not give much energy, so sloths save energy by moving slowly and sleeping a lot.

b.title: Slow and Steady Survives
text: Every October 20, wildlife groups celebrate International Sloth Day, a date created in Colombia in 2010 to raise awareness about one of the rainforest's most unusual animals.
Sloths live in the treetops of Central and South America. There are two main groups, two-toed and three-toed sloths, and both spend nearly their whole lives hanging upside down from branches.

Their famous slowness is not laziness but a clever survival strategy. Sloths live on a diet of leaves, which contain very little energy, so their bodies run at an extremely low speed — they even digest food slowly, sometimes over several days.
Moving slowly also keeps them safe. Eagles and big cats notice movement, and a sloth that barely moves is hard to spot, especially since algae growing in its fur gives it a greenish colour.
Surprisingly, sloths are good swimmers, and they climb down to the ground only about once a week — mainly to go to the toilet.
Their biggest dangers today come from people: forests cleared for farms and roads, electric power lines, and illegal trading of babies as pets.

c.title: The Wisdom of Slowness
text: In a culture that prizes speed, the sloth is an easy joke: the patron saint of laziness, a creature that seems to have opted out of effort altogether. International Sloth Day, held every October 20, invites us to look again.

A sloth's pace is not a flaw but an exquisitely tuned economy. Its diet of tough, low-calorie leaves would starve a more ambitious animal, so the sloth simply spends less — a slow metabolism, little muscle, and a body temperature that drifts with the air around it.
Even its stillness is strategic. Harpy eagles and jaguars hunt by detecting motion; an animal that barely moves, its fur tinted green by algae, all but disappears into the canopy.

Yet the very trait that has served sloths for millions of years leaves them helpless against modern threats. They cannot outrun a bulldozer, and as roads and power lines cut through the forest, an animal designed for patience meets a world that has run out of it.

Perhaps that is the day's quiet lesson. Success need not mean doing more, faster; sometimes it means fitting your life precisely to what your surroundings can give — and asking whether we are leaving room for creatures who live by a different clock.

a.title: The Man Who Started the Nobel Prize

b.title: From Dynamite to the Nobel Prize
text: Each October the world waits for the Nobel Prize announcements. October 21 is the birthday of the man behind them: Alfred Nobel, born in Stockholm in 1833.
Nobel grew up partly in Russia, spoke several languages and became a gifted chemist. Over his life he collected 355 patents, but one invention made his fortune: dynamite, patented in 1867.

Dynamite made the dangerous liquid nitroglycerin much safer to handle, and it transformed the building of mines, tunnels and railways. Yet it was also used in weapons, and Nobel himself owned factories that made arms.

In 1888, when his brother Ludvig died, a French newspaper reportedly mixed up the brothers and printed Alfred's obituary instead, calling him a 'merchant of death'. Historians are not sure how much this shocked him, but the story is often told.

In 1895, in Paris, Nobel signed a will that left most of his huge fortune to fund prizes for those who had brought 'the greatest benefit to humankind' in physics, chemistry, medicine, literature and peace.
He died in Italy on December 10, 1896. The first prizes were awarded in 1901, and they are still presented on December 10 every year.

c.title: A Fortune in Search of a Conscience
text: Few names are as firmly attached to virtue as Nobel's — which is a curious fate for a man who made his fortune from explosives. Born in Stockholm on October 21, 1833, Alfred Nobel was a restless polyglot chemist whose 355 patents included the one that defined him: dynamite.

His invention tamed nitroglycerin, a liquid so unstable that it had killed workers, including Nobel's own younger brother in an 1864 factory blast. Packed into a safer form, it blasted open mines, canals and railways across the industrial world — and, inevitably, found its way into war.

Legend holds that in 1888 a French newspaper, mistaking his brother Ludvig's death for his own, branded him 'the merchant of death'. The anecdote is almost too neat, and historians treat it with caution; still, it captures a real tension in a man who wrote poetry, never married, and seemed uneasy with the source of his wealth.

Whatever his motives, his will of 1895 was radical. It bypassed his relatives and directed most of his estate towards prizes, regardless of nationality, for those who had conferred 'the greatest benefit to humankind'.

More than a century later, the prizes are less a monument to Nobel than a standing argument about what benefit means — and a reminder that how a fortune is spent can, in the end, redefine how it was made.

b.title: Peru's Citadel Above the Clouds
text: Perched on a narrow ridge in the Andes, about 2,430 metres above sea level, Machu Picchu is one of the most breathtaking places on Earth.
The Inca built it in the mid-1400s, probably as a royal estate for the emperor Pachacuti. Less than a century later the site was abandoned, around the time the Spanish conquered the Inca Empire.

Because the Spanish never found it, Machu Picchu survived largely intact. Local farmers always knew it was there, but it became world-famous after the American explorer Hiram Bingham publicised it in 1911.
Its stonework is remarkable. Builders shaped granite blocks so precisely that they fit together without mortar, and the walls have survived centuries of earthquakes.
In 1983 the site became a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Today visitors arrive by train and bus from Cusco, or hike the famous Inca Trail, which usually takes four days.
Popularity brings problems, however. To prevent damage, Peru limits daily visitor numbers and sets fixed routes through the ruins.

c.title: The City That Was Never Lost
text: Machu Picchu is routinely called a 'lost city', a phrase that says more about the outside world than about the place itself. Set on a saddle of rock some 2,430 metres up in the Peruvian Andes, it was never truly lost to the people who farmed the slopes below.

Built in the mid-fifteenth century, most likely as an estate for the Inca ruler Pachacuti, it was occupied for less than a hundred years. When the Spanish conquest shattered the empire, the site simply fell quiet — and, crucially, it escaped the colonisers' attention, sparing it the destruction suffered by so many Inca temples.

What survives is an argument in stone. Granite blocks were shaped to fit so closely that no mortar was needed, and the slightly flexible joints have let the walls ride out earthquakes that toppled later buildings.

Hiram Bingham's 1911 expedition turned the site into an international icon, but it also reflected an era in which foreign 'discovery' erased local knowledge, and artefacts he removed were returned to Peru only in this century.

Today the danger is love rather than neglect. With crowds pressing on fragile terraces, Peru caps daily entries and fixes routes — a reminder that a place can survive centuries of isolation and still be worn away by admiration.

a.title: A Day for a Very Big Number
text: October 23 is Mole Day. It is not about the little animal! It is a day for chemistry.
Everything is made of atoms. Atoms are so small that we cannot see them, even with a normal microscope.
Because atoms are tiny, scientists count them in big groups. One group is called a mole.
One mole is about 602,000,000,000,000,000,000,000 things. People write it as 6.02 × 10²³.
That is why Mole Day is on 10/23, from 6:02 in the morning to 6:02 in the evening.

b.title: Why Chemists Celebrate at 6:02
text: Every year on October 23, chemistry classrooms celebrate Mole Day. The party runs from 6:02 a.m. to 6:02 p.m., and the timing is a clue to what it honours.
In chemistry, a mole is not an animal but a unit for counting particles. Just as a 'dozen' means twelve, a mole means about 6.02 × 10²³ — a six followed by twenty-three digits.
This value is known as Avogadro's number, named after the Italian scientist Amedeo Avogadro, whose ideas in the early 1800s helped explain how gases behave.
Why such an enormous number? Atoms are unimaginably small. A single sip of water — about 18 grams — contains roughly one mole of water molecules.
Using moles lets chemists connect the invisible world of atoms to amounts they can actually weigh on a scale, which is essential for medicine, cooking chemistry and industry.
Mole Day began in American schools in the 1980s, and today teachers mark it with experiments, mole-shaped cakes and plenty of terrible puns.

c.title: A Bridge Between Two Worlds
text: On October 23, from 6:02 in the morning until 6:02 at night, chemistry teachers indulge in a ritual of cakes, costumes and shameless puns. Mole Day is silly by design, but the number it celebrates is one of the quiet pillars of modern science.

A mole is simply a counting unit — like a dozen, only vastly larger. It stands for roughly 6.02 × 10²³ particles, a quantity named in honour of Amedeo Avogadro, the Italian scientist who proposed in 1811 that equal volumes of gas hold equal numbers of molecules.

Avogadro's idea was largely ignored in his lifetime. Only decades after his death did chemists recognise how neatly it untangled the confusion over atomic weights, and the constant bearing his name was measured with real precision only much later.

The mole's genius lies in translation. Atoms are far too small to count or weigh individually, yet a mole of any substance has a mass in grams that matches its atomic or molecular weight. A sip of water, about eighteen grams, contains a mole of water molecules — a number larger than the grains of sand on many beaches combined.
Mole Day, then, celebrates a bridge: between the invisible and the measurable, and between an overlooked idea and its eventual vindication.

a.title: Almost Gone for Good
text: October 24 is World Polio Day. Polio is a disease caused by a virus. It mostly makes young children sick.
Polio can hurt the body's nerves. Some children cannot walk again after they get it.
In the past, polio was common all over the world. Parents were very afraid of it.
Then scientists made vaccines. One was a shot, and later one was a few drops in the mouth. The drops are cheap and easy to give.
Since then, millions of children have got the vaccine. Polio is now almost gone. Taiwan has been free of polio for many years.
But the virus is still found in a few places. World Polio Day reminds us to finish the job.

b.title: The Last Mile Against Polio
text: Every October 24, health workers mark World Polio Day, an awareness day started by Rotary International to honour the fight against one of history's most feared childhood diseases.
Polio is caused by a virus that spreads mainly through contaminated water and hands. In a small number of cases it attacks the nerves and can cause lifelong paralysis.

In the early 1950s, epidemics left thousands of children unable to walk each year. In 1955 a vaccine developed by a team led by Jonas Salk was declared safe and effective, and a few years later Albert Sabin's oral vaccine — given as drops — made mass vaccination cheap and simple.

In 1988 the World Health Organization and its partners launched a global campaign to end polio. Back then, the disease paralysed an estimated 350,000 children a year. Since then, cases have fallen by more than 99 percent.
Wild poliovirus now survives in only two countries, Pakistan and Afghanistan, where conflict and distrust make it hard to reach every child.
Taiwan was certified polio-free as part of its region in 2000. Experts warn, though, that as long as the virus exists anywhere, every country must keep vaccinating.

c.title: Why the Last One Percent Is the Hardest
text: There are few public-health stories as triumphant, or as unfinished, as polio's. World Polio Day, marked each October 24, celebrates a disease driven to the brink of extinction — and admits how stubbornly it clings on.

In the first half of the twentieth century, summer polio epidemics emptied swimming pools and terrified parents; the virus, usually silent, occasionally invaded the nervous system and left children paralysed. The 1955 announcement that Jonas Salk's injected vaccine worked was greeted almost like the end of a war, and Albert Sabin's oral drops later made immunisation affordable on a mass scale.

When the Global Polio Eradication Initiative began in 1988, polio paralysed an estimated 350,000 children a year in more than 125 countries. Cases have since fallen by over 99 percent, and wild virus persists in just two, Pakistan and Afghanistan.

Yet the final fraction is the most expensive and the most fragile. The remaining cases sit where conflict blocks vaccinators, where rumours breed suspicion, and where a single missed child can seed a new outbreak.

Eradication, after all, is unforgiving arithmetic: ninety-nine percent is not a near-success but an unfinished task. Only smallpox has ever been fully defeated in humans; polio's last mile will test whether the world can sustain attention long after a crisis stops feeling urgent.

a.title: One Day for the World
text: October 24 is United Nations Day. It celebrates the day the United Nations, or UN, began in 1945.
The UN started after the Second World War. Countries were tired of fighting and wanted to keep peace.
Today, almost every country in the world is a member. They meet and talk instead of fighting.
The UN does many things. It helps people after disasters, sends food and medicine, and protects children's rights.

b.title: When Nations Talk
text: Each year on 24 October, the world marks United Nations Day, the anniversary of the day in 1945 when the UN officially came into being.
The organisation was born from the ruins of the Second World War. Its founders, having seen two world wars in thirty years, hoped that a place where countries could talk might stop a third.
Today the UN has 193 member states — nearly every nation on Earth. They gather in New York to debate, to vote, and, when they can, to agree.
The UN's work reaches far beyond politics. Its agencies feed refugees, fight diseases, care for children, protect human rights, and coordinate action on climate change.
It is far from perfect. Powerful countries can block decisions, and the UN often cannot force anyone to obey. Critics say it is too slow and too weak.
Yet its defenders point to a simple fact: since 1945 there has been no third world war. Imperfect as it is, a place where enemies must at least talk may be worth keeping.

c.title: An Imperfect Necessity
text: On 24 October the world observes United Nations Day, commemorating the moment in 1945 when a charter signed in San Francisco brought the organisation formally to life.

The UN was an act of exhausted hope. Its architects, surveying a planet twice shattered by world war within a single generation, built not a world government but something humbler: a permanent table around which states, however hostile, would be obliged to sit.

Judged against its loftiest ideals, the UN disappoints. Its Security Council can be paralysed by a single veto; its resolutions are often ignored; its peacekeepers arrive late, or not at all. To its critics it is a mere talking shop, long on words and short on power.

Judged more modestly, the record looks different. UN agencies vaccinate children, shelter refugees, monitor elections, and feed tens of millions; its very existence has made war between great powers, if not impossible, at least harder to begin. Absence, not presence, is often the truer measure of such an institution.
That may be the paradox worth marking each October: an organisation too weak to command and too useful to abandon — an imperfect necessity in a world that has, so far, invented nothing better.

b.title: The Artist Who Kept Reinventing Himself
text: Born in Málaga, Spain, on October 25, 1881, Pablo Picasso is often called the most influential artist of the twentieth century.
Trained by his father, an art teacher, he showed remarkable skill as a teenager. But he soon grew bored with simply copying what he saw.

In his early twenties he moved between Barcelona and Paris. After the death of a close friend, he painted poor and lonely people in cold shades of blue — the Blue Period — and later turned to warmer pinks and circus performers in his Rose Period.

Around 1907 he painted Les Demoiselles d'Avignon, a shocking picture of sharp, broken shapes. With his friend Georges Braque he then developed Cubism, a style that shows an object from several viewpoints at once.
In 1937, after German and Italian planes bombed the Spanish town of Guernica during the Spanish Civil War, Picasso painted Guernica, a huge black-and-white protest against the horror of war.
He kept experimenting with painting, sculpture and pottery until his death in 1973, leaving behind tens of thousands of works.

c.title: Why Picasso Painted Faces from Two Sides
text: It is a familiar complaint in galleries: 'My child could paint that.' Pablo Picasso, born in Málaga on October 25, 1881, would hardly have been offended; by his teens he could already draw with academic polish, and he spent the rest of his long life deliberately unlearning it.

His early work was melancholy and lyrical — the cold blues of beggars and outcasts, then the softer roses of acrobats. But around 1907, with Les Demoiselles d'Avignon, he broke with the idea that a painting must imitate a single, fixed view of the world.

Cubism, which he developed alongside Georges Braque, fractured objects into planes and showed them from several angles at once. A face might appear in profile and from the front simultaneously, not because Picasso could not see, but because he wanted to paint what we know about an object, not merely how it looks from one spot.

That restlessness became a method. He moved from painting to collage, sculpture and ceramics, and in Guernica (1937) he turned the bombing of a Basque town into an enduring image of civilian suffering.

Picasso's legacy is complicated, including how he treated the people closest to him. Yet his central provocation endures: that seeing is not a passive act, and that an artist's job may be to show us the world in pieces so that we look at it again.

a.title: One Game, One Set of Rules

On October 26, 1863, a group of men met in London. They started the Football Association, or the FA.

b.title: How a Pub Meeting Shaped the World's Game
text: On the evening of October 26, 1863, a group of men met at the Freemasons' Tavern in London. They represented a dozen clubs and schools, and they had one goal: to agree on a single set of rules for football.
At the time, the game was chaotic. Each English school had its own version. Some allowed players to pick up the ball and run; some allowed 'hacking' — deliberately kicking an opponent's shins.
Led by Ebenezer Morley, a solicitor who had founded his own club, the group formed the Football Association. Over several more meetings they debated what the game should look like.
The biggest arguments were about handling and hacking. When the FA banned both, a few clubs walked out, and their style of play later developed into rugby.
The first Laws of the Game were published in December 1863. Many details have changed since, but the core idea — a kicking game with shared rules — spread around the world.
Even the word 'soccer' comes from the FA: it is a playful short form of 'association football'.

c.title: The Invention of a Common Language
text: It is easy to forget that the world's most popular sport was once barely a single sport at all. Before October 26, 1863, 'football' in England was a family of local customs, each school jealously guarding its own peculiar version.

That evening, representatives of a dozen clubs gathered at the Freemasons' Tavern in London and founded the Football Association. Their ambition was modest and practical: a shared code so that teams from different places could actually play one another.

The negotiations exposed a deeper divide. Some clubs prized handling the ball and 'hacking', the bruising practice of kicking an opponent's shins, as tests of manliness; others saw them as obstacles to skill. When the FA outlawed both, the dissenters withdrew, and their tradition hardened into rugby.

The Laws of the Game published that December were brief and, by modern standards, strange. Yet they established something more durable than any single rule: the principle that a game could belong to everyone only if everyone agreed to play it the same way.

From that principle grew leagues, international fixtures and eventually FIFA. A pub meeting about kicking and shins turned out to be an early experiment in global cooperation — a common language spoken with the feet.

b.title: The World Tree and Its Gods
text: More than a thousand years ago, the Norse peoples of Scandinavia told rich myths about gods, giants, and the fate of the world. The Vikings carried these stories across the seas.
At the centre stood Yggdrasil, an immense tree whose roots and branches linked nine worlds — the home of the gods, the land of humans, the realm of the dead, and more.

The gods themselves were powerful but far from perfect. Odin, the one-eyed king, hungered for wisdom and traded an eye to drink from a well of knowledge. Thor defended the gods with his thunderous hammer, Mjölnir.
And then there was Loki, a shape-shifting trickster, sometimes helpful and often dangerous, whose schemes drove many of the tales.
Unlike many mythologies, the Norse one had a clear ending in mind: Ragnarok, a final battle in which gods and monsters would destroy one another and the world would sink beneath the sea.
Yet even this end was not truly final. From the ruins, the myths promised, a green new world would rise, and life would begin again.

c.title: A Mythology That Expected the End
text: Most mythologies tell how the world began; the Norse myths are unusual in dwelling, with grim relish, on how it will end. For the peoples of early Scandinavia, even the gods were mortal, and doom was written into the structure of things.

Their cosmos hung upon Yggdrasil, a vast world-tree binding nine realms. Among its branches moved gods who were strikingly human — Odin, who sacrificed an eye and hung himself upon the tree for wisdom; Thor, strong and short-tempered; Loki, whose cunning was both the gods' tool and their undoing.

What distinguishes these stories is their honesty about loss. The gods know that Ragnarok is coming — that they will fall, that Loki's children will break free, that the sun will be swallowed — and they fight on regardless.

There is a bleak courage in this. To act well while knowing you cannot win is, in the Norse imagination, close to the very definition of heroism; glory lies not in victory but in how one meets the end.
And yet the myths refuse final despair. After the fire and flood, a new earth rises, green and clean. Even a mythology braced for the end could not quite give up on beginning again.

a.title: The Day We Celebrate Our First Language
text: Every year on February 21, the world celebrates International Mother Language Day.
Your mother language is the first language you learn at home, from your family.
There are thousands of languages on Earth. Each one carries a culture, stories, and a way of seeing the world.
UNESCO, part of the United Nations, says children learn best when they can first study in their own language.
Around the world, teachers make books and lessons in local languages. In some places, they also teach in sign language so more children can join in.
Learning English is wonderful — and so is keeping the language your grandparents speak. Every language is worth protecting.

b.title: Mother Tongues, Open Doors
text: On 21 February each year, UNESCO marks International Mother Language Day. In 2026, it focused on the role of young people in multilingual education.
A 'mother tongue' is the language you grow up speaking at home. For many children, though, school begins in a different language they barely understand.
Research shows that children learn to read and think more easily when they start in their own language. A familiar language is a bridge, not a barrier.

Across the world, projects are building that bridge. In Indonesia, young people are trained to teach in Indigenous languages. In Thailand, award-winning digital tools include features in sign language.
One organisation, active in 29 countries, publishes storybooks in local languages and makes versions in braille and sign language, so no child is left out.
Speaking more than one language is a gift. Learning a global language like English opens the world — while keeping your mother tongue keeps you connected to who you are.

c.title: The Case for Mother Tongues
text: Each 21 February, UNESCO's International Mother Language Day celebrates the world's linguistic diversity. The 2026 edition spotlighted young people as leaders in multilingual education.

A mother tongue is more than a tool for communication; it is woven into identity, memory, and belonging. Yet millions of children begin school in a language they scarcely speak, and many fall behind before they have truly begun.
Decades of research point the same way: pupils who first learn to read in a familiar language understand more, stay in school longer, and later pick up additional languages more easily.

Around the globe, educators are putting this into practice. In Indonesia, local youth are trained to teach in Indigenous tongues; in Thailand, award-winning digital tools weave in sign language; and in India, thousands of sign-language videos now span more than twenty official languages.
A charity working across twenty-nine countries prints storybooks in local languages and adapts them into braille and sign language, so that disability and poverty need not mean exclusion.

None of this competes with learning powerful world languages such as English. The goal is addition, not subtraction: to open global doors while keeping alive the languages that carry a community's history.

topic: "LO": The First Message on the Internet
zh: 「LO」：網路史上第一則訊息

a.title: Two Letters That Changed the World
text: Today we send messages every day. But do you know the first message on the internet? It had only two letters: LO.
On October 29, 1969, a student in Los Angeles sat at a big computer. He wanted to send the word LOGIN to another computer far away.
He typed L, and it arrived. He typed O, and it arrived. Then he typed G — and the system crashed!
So the first message was just LO, like the start of 'hello'. About an hour later, the full word worked.
That small network was called ARPANET. Over many years, it grew into the internet we use today.
Now billions of people go online. It all began with two little letters.

b.title: The Night the Internet Said Its First Word
text: At about 10:30 p.m. on October 29, 1969, a student programmer named Charley Kline sat at a terminal at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA).
His team, led by computer scientist Leonard Kleinrock, was testing ARPANET, a new network funded by the US government to connect research computers in different places.
Kline's goal was simple: log in to a computer at the Stanford Research Institute, about 560 kilometres away. He began typing the word LOGIN while talking to a colleague at the other end by telephone.
'Did you get the L?' 'Yes.' 'Did you get the O?' 'Yes.' Then, as he typed the G, the Stanford system crashed. The first message ever sent across the network was therefore 'LO'.
After a quick fix, the full login worked about an hour later. By the end of 1969, four computers were connected.
ARPANET kept growing and introduced ideas, such as breaking messages into small packets, that still power the internet today.

c.title: An Accidental Hello
text: History rarely announces itself, and on the night of October 29, 1969, it arrived as a crash. At a terminal in a UCLA laboratory, the student programmer Charley Kline set out to log in to a computer at the Stanford Research Institute, some 560 kilometres north, over a fledgling network called ARPANET.

The procedure was almost comically low-tech. Kline typed while a colleague in Stanford confirmed each character over the telephone. The L arrived; so did the O. On the G, the remote system collapsed, and the first message transmitted across what would become the internet was an unintended 'LO'.
Leonard Kleinrock, who led the UCLA team, later relished the accident: no one could have scripted a more fitting first word than an abrupt 'lo', as in 'lo and behold'.

Funded by the US Defense Department to link scattered research computers, ARPANET was built on packet switching, which chops data into small, independently routed pieces. The design was meant for resilience and efficient sharing, not for billions of users.

That gap between intention and outcome is the real lesson of the night. The engineers were solving a narrow technical problem; they could not foresee social media, online classrooms or misinformation. Small experiments, it turns out, can grow far beyond the imagination of the people who run them.

a.title: Martians on the Radio
text: On October 30, 1938, the night before Halloween, many Americans were listening to the radio.
A radio show told a famous story called The War of the Worlds. In the story, Martians land in New Jersey and attack!
The show sounded like real news. There were 'reporters', loud noises and scared voices.
The next day, newspapers said that thousands of people were very frightened. They said people ran into the streets.
But later, historians studied it again. They found that not many people were really scared. The newspapers made the story bigger.

b.title: The Panic That Wasn't Quite a Panic
text: On the evening of October 30, 1938, CBS radio broadcast a drama by Orson Welles and his Mercury Theatre: an adaptation of H. G. Wells's novel The War of the Worlds.

Instead of telling the story in the usual way, the show was written like a series of breaking news reports. Music was interrupted by 'bulletins' describing explosions on Mars and a strange object landing at Grover's Mill, New Jersey.
The next morning, newspapers across America reported that the broadcast had caused mass hysteria, with listeners fleeing their homes in terror.

The legend has lasted for decades. But many historians now argue that the panic was greatly exaggerated. Ratings suggest relatively few people were even listening, and most of those knew it was a play.
Why would newspapers exaggerate? Radio was a fast-growing rival for advertising money, and a story showing radio as dangerous and irresponsible served their interests.
So the real lesson of The War of the Worlds may be less about gullible listeners and more about how a dramatic story can spread — even when the facts are thin.

c.title: A Hoax About a Hoax
text: Few media legends are as durable as the night America supposedly believed it was being invaded by Mars. On October 30, 1938, Orson Welles's Mercury Theatre adapted H. G. Wells's The War of the Worlds for CBS radio, cleverly disguising the story as a sequence of urgent news bulletins.

By the next morning, front pages were thick with accounts of terrified listeners crowding roads and churches. The episode became a textbook example of mass credulity — proof, it seemed, of the hypnotic power of the new medium.

Later scholarship has been far more sceptical. Audience ratings indicate that only a small share of radio owners were tuned in, and contemporary reports of chaos rest largely on anecdote. Some listeners were certainly alarmed, but the nationwide hysteria appears to have been largely a newspaper creation.
The motive is not hard to find. Print journalism was losing advertisers to radio, and a tale of irresponsible broadcasting flattered newspapers as the sober guardians of truth.

The irony is delicious: the enduring story about people being fooled by fake news was itself, in large part, fake news. In an age of viral rumours, the episode is worth remembering less as a warning about credulous audiences than as a reminder to ask who benefits when a sensational story is told.
